Controlled generated 1s · geometry-assisted registration · no pixel resampling

Is position disguising a simpler direction pattern?

First, a correction about the previous experiment. Its large libraries were linear SVD patterns. They reconstructed directions supplied by the existing analytic renderer. We did not learn hundreds of piecewise motion functions. The exact nonlinear rules we found link width to horizontal shift and height to center shifts; the five direction families are not isolated rule collections.

This experiment moves direction coefficients into a common boundary frame before fitting SVD. It then moves the decoded coefficients back into the original 28 × 28 image, so success is measured in the original pixels. Alignment must be stored too: three numbers for centerline registration, five for full boundary registration.

1 · The same operation at different starting images

Each source pixel is ink coverage: white means 0, black means 1. Its horizontal-center direction has signed pixel changes: red gains ink, blue loses ink. We split that map into upper-left, upper-right, lower-left and lower-right patches, aligning each side and cap by whole-pixel moves.

2 · Position was hiding a substantial amount of simplicity

The raw ranks above use the original 384 training images. The earlier experiment used additional coverage to reach ranks 260, 265, 95, 267 and 260. Registered maps have fewer patterns and their training span covers unseen registered patterns more effectively. A large reduction is not the same as a collapse to one or two shared patterns.

What is counted: for one direction, store five source-image-derived geometry numbers plus its k SVD coefficients. The five families can share those geometry numbers. Four patches contain 448 slots, including zeros; a fixed trained basis is stored by the decoder. Every integer shift and partition follows from those five numbers, with no per-row position list supplied.

How much do the rules overlap?

The earlier full height library lies within the width library’s linear span. The full horizontal and lean libraries span the same space to numerical precision. These libraries pool vectors from many source images; this does not make two knobs interchangeable at one image.

The exact nonlinear identities are more specific. With the five geometry numbers shared, the aligned horizontal, height and lean fields reconstruct all five direction maps: width is half the absolute horizontal map, and vertical is tan(lean) times horizontal plus the signed top/bottom caps from height. This shared decoder stores 208 scalars including geometry across the five fields. It is still an encoder of observed directions, and the shared mathematical rules are supplied.

3 · Does it survive decoding back to the original pixels?

The 512 random and 1,024 near-edge states here are fresh tests. Error is the reconstructed direction’s L2 error divided by the true direction’s L2 length. Near-edge sampling is separate from exact renderer events, where the two one-sided directions may differ.

5 · Compression is not yet prediction from the image alone

For the near-exact reconstruction test, coefficients are computed from the true direction. To test a different claim, we fitted a separate RBF model that sees only the five geometry numbers recovered from the source image, predicts the aligned direction, and decodes it. Its bandwidth and regularization were chosen using 128 validation images.

Vertical center31.8%56.3%63.9%
Height34.8%62.8%70.3%
Width22.9%45.4%48.2%

The source-only predictor remains imperfect. Near-exact compression does not establish a learned function that predicts the knob’s direction from the state. The five geometry numbers plus the known analytic renderer already provide that function as a supplied baseline; this experiment does not rediscover it.

6 · Joint moves and exact boundaries

We tested simultaneous changes by combining all five decoded directions at 512 fresh smooth states. We also compared true and decoded first-order predictions against rendered finite joint moves at normalized sizes from 10⁻⁵ to 0.1. Curvature and event crossings produce finite-step error even with exact local directions; those errors are listed separately in the results.

At five exact event/intersection states, we tested both one-sided directions for all five knobs. A single source-side chart failed on 3 of those 50 vectors, reaching 100% relative error. Choosing the registration chart on the requested side of the event reduced the worst error to 2.07e-15, without adding learned patterns. This adds one side-selection bit for a requested one-sided direction; grid-rounding ties use tolerance 10⁻¹⁰. A separate audit of 320 one-sided directions at 32 new event states had worst relative error 2.35e-15, using the same basis and side-aware chart. The derivative limits were checked against one-sided rendered moves. These tests include sides just outside the default sampling box, supported by the renderer. Float32 source-image alignment is also tested separately. For the 320 exact-event audit directions its worst relative error was 8.01e-01; tiny recovery errors can affect an exact chart decision.

What remains after integer registration?

The stroke’s position relative to fractional pixel boundaries still changes. So do the sixteen subrow edge crossings, cap placement within a row, and the lever-arm weights in the lean direction. Whole-pixel alignment removes location variation but preserves those effects. This result measures one reversible registration; it does not rule out a more effective nonlinear representation.
